questions.question: Why add an input classifier before an agent rather than rely on its final answer alone?
options: It guarantees that every later action is harmless
It replaces the model's output checks and tool policy
It can route or block risky requests before downstream actions
It proves that the user's intent matches the request
questions.explanation: An input classifier can reject or route a risky request before it reaches downstream reasoning, but it cannot guarantee all later actions are harmless. Tool permissions and output checks cover risks the input rail cannot see.

questions.question: What capability does Llama Guard 4 add relative to Guard 3 in the lesson?
options: Multimodal image-and-text input with categories expanded to S1–S14
Colang-defined conversation-flow rails that persist across turns
A guarantee that adversarial bypasses have zero success
An eight-language input/output classifier with a 13-hazard taxonomy
questions.explanation: Guard 4 adds image-and-text input and extends the taxonomy to S14; Guard 3 is the 13-hazard, eight-language model. Neither version guarantees zero bypasses, so the absolute-guarantee option overstates a classifier.

questions.question: Which behavior separates a NeMo dialog rail from input and output rails?
options: It enforces a conversation flow constraint across turns.
It classifies one model response after generation.
It normalizes Unicode before input classification.
It classifies one user request before generation.
questions.explanation: Dialog rails preserve a rule across turns, while input and output rails classify one user or model turn. Unicode normalization is preprocessing, not the conversation-flow behavior that distinguishes Colang rails.

questions.question: The raw classifier misses a forbidden phrase split by zero-width characters. Which normalization strategy does the code demonstrate?
options: Apply NFKC, map selected homoglyphs, then remove selected invisible code points.
Map selected homoglyphs but preserve zero-width characters in the text.
Delete every non-ASCII character before classification, including legitimate text.
Apply NFKC but retain invisible characters and homoglyphs before classifying.
questions.explanation: NFKC, selected homoglyph mapping, and removal of selected invisible code points expose this split phrase to the classifier. Deleting every non-ASCII character would also destroy legitimate multilingual content.

questions.question: An input classifier accepts a request, but the generated response contains a secret-shaped token. Which rail can inspect it?
options: An output rail that classifies the generated response for sensitive patterns.
A second input rail that repeats classification of the original request.
A Unicode normalizer applied before the model reads the request.
A dialog rail that checks the user turn but skips model output.
questions.explanation: An output rail scans generated text for secret-key or API-token patterns after generation. Repeating only the input check cannot catch sensitive content that first appears in the model response.

questions.question: A classifier catches obvious misuse but misses a paraphrase or multi-turn attack. What architecture follows the lesson?
options: Treat the classifier as a complete security boundary
Allow the model to change the classifier taxonomy
Combine it with constitutional and runtime controls
Remove action budgets because the request was classified
questions.explanation: Classifiers catch some obvious misuse but can miss paraphrases and multi-turn compositions, so combine them with constitutional behavior, runtime permissions/budgets, and human review. A taxonomy alone is not a complete security boundary.
